title: The efficacy of upgrading rural drinking water treatment in karst areas of Chongqing: simultaneous removal of conventional pollutants and microplastics
content: Rural drinking water safety is a critical issue in China's public health sector. This study focused on typical small-scale rural water treatment plants in the karst region of southeastern Chongqing, Southwest China, and systematically compared the treatment performance of the conventional simplified coagulation-natural sedimentation-sand filtration process with that of the upgraded combined grid-flocculation-inclined tube sedimentation-submerged ultrafiltration (GF-TS-SUF) process. The removal efficiency of the processes was quantitatively assessed based on conventional parameters such as turbidity, color, iron, manganese, permanganate index, nitrate (NO3−), as well as microplastics (abundance, morphology, size, polymer type), and correlations among parameters were explored. The results showed that the GF-TS-SUF process achieved substantially higher purification efficiency in this case study, with an effluent turbidity of 0.28 ± 0.02 NTU, a color of 3 ± 1 PCU, iron and manganese levels below detection limits, and a permanganate index of 1.58 ± 0.09 mg L−1. The GF-TS-SUF process exhibited excellent microplastic retention performance, with only trace amounts of microplastics detected in the final effluent, indicating that the vast majority of influent microplastics were effectively removed. Exploratory analysis showed strong co-variation between microplastic abundance and turbidity, permanganate index and other conventional parameters across treatment stages, indicating that these readily measured indicators may serve as a useful preliminary operational reference for tracking microplastic removal. As these variables decline together along the treatment train, this relationship should nonetheless be regarded as exploratory and remains pending independent validation. This single-site case study suggests the potential feasibility of the GF-TS-SUF process for the simultaneous removal of conventional and emerging pollutants at the studied rural water treatment plant and provides a preliminary reference for other small-scale water plants with similar source-water characteristics and operational conditions.
